lesson.title: Splitting the Charge: Capacitors in Series
lesson.summary: Series capacitors share the same charge rather than the same voltage, which makes their combined capacitance smaller than any one of them alone.
lesson.body:
A series circuit chains components one after another along a single path, forcing the same current to flow through every element in the loop, a rule you already know from series circuits built with resistors. Capacitors do not pass a steady current through their internal gap, but when charge is actively flowing onto and off of a chain of series capacitors, that flow travels through a single path too, which means the same amount of charge is deposited onto one plate of every capacitor in the chain, and pulled from the facing plate of its neighbor, in equal measure. The result is that every capacitor in a series chain ends up holding the identical amount of charge Q, even though the capacitors themselves may have very different capacitance values.

Because each capacitor holds the same charge Q but has its own capacitance, each one develops its own voltage, following V equals Q divided by C. The total voltage across the whole chain is the sum of the individual voltages, V-total equals V1 plus V2 plus further terms, which expands to Q divided by C1, plus Q divided by C2, and so on. Since V-total also equals Q divided by C-total by definition, dividing both sides by Q leaves 1 divided by C-total equals 1 divided by C1, plus 1 divided by C2, plus further terms. This is the same reciprocal, add-the-inverses pattern used for resistors in parallel, and it means the combined capacitance of a series chain is always smaller than the smallest individual capacitor in that chain.

Take two capacitors in series, C1 at 4 microfarads and C2 at 12 microfarads. Using the reciprocal formula: 1 divided by C-total equals 1 divided by 4, plus 1 divided by 12. Converting to a common denominator of 12, that is 3 divided by 12 plus 1 divided by 12, which equals 4 divided by 12, or 1 divided by 3. So C-total equals 3 microfarads. For exactly two capacitors, the same answer comes faster from the product-over-sum shortcut: C1 times C2, divided by C1 plus C2, which is 4 times 12 divided by 4 plus 12, or 48 divided by 16, equal to 3 microfarads, confirming the reciprocal method.

Now connect that pair to a 10 volt source and see how the voltage splits. The total charge delivered is Q equals C-total times V, so Q equals 3 microfarads times 10 volts, equal to 30 microcoulombs, and that same 30 microcoulombs sits on both C1 and C2. The individual voltages follow: V1 equals Q divided by C1, which is 30 microcoulombs divided by 4 microfarads, equal to 7.5 volts, and V2 equals Q divided by C2, which is 30 microcoulombs divided by 12 microfarads, equal to 2.5 volts. Adding them back together, 7.5 plus 2.5 equals 10 volts, matching the source exactly. Notice that the smaller capacitor, C1, ended up carrying the larger share of the voltage, the opposite of what happens with resistors in series, where the larger resistance takes the larger voltage share.

Designers put capacitors in series deliberately for this voltage splitting effect. If a single capacitor cannot survive the full voltage of an application, chaining several in series lets each one see only its fraction of the total, at the cost of reducing the overall capacitance and needing to account carefully for how unevenly that voltage divides, since a manufacturing mismatch between capacitors can push one of them well past its safe rating even while the total looks fine on paper.
